prompt:
A grand establishing landscape on a clear, bright morning, full of life: the sunward face of the dwarven mountains, the most beautifully made place in the world. Tiny dwarves tend the rooftop vegetable gardens and walk the stairways; smoke rises from chimneys; barges come and go at the harbour below, where dockworkers swing cargo. Homes and gate share one architecture: plain stone, clean horizontal lines, bold cantilevers.

Setting: the whole sunward face of a great mountain, seen from across the valley. The homes are hundreds of plain rectangular stone blocks stacked and offset up the slope in the spirit of Habitat 67: each block shifted from the one below so that every roof is the garden of the home above, blocks bridging and cantilevering over each other, open-air walkways and stairs threading between them, bands of glass windows. Every rooftop garden grows food in perfectly straight rows: cabbages, beans climbing poles, herbs, squash, espaliered fruit trees, beehives. Below and between the homes, tier after tier of green barley terraces cascade down the slope. In the centre a huge waterfall pours out of the rock, and the great gate is ONE great building over and into it, the boldest, most daring structure on the mountain: long, wide horizontal stone floors cantilevered far out across the falling water like Fallingwater made monumental, in the same clean style as the homes. Stone channels carry water from the falls across the terraces and turn the waterwheels of forges, whose smoke rises from neat openings in the cliff. At the mountain's foot, where the falls become a navigable river, a busy river harbour: long, plain stone quays, precise counterweighted timber-and-steel cranes, flat river barges unloading wine barrels, fish, grain and timber from across the world and loading crates of plain polished steel armour and swords bound downriver. The river runs on through pine forest toward the distant lowlands; snow-capped peaks above.

The dwarven mountains look: an alpine range of grey stone, dark pine forest and snow-capped peaks at the headwaters of a river. Dwarven architecture is beauty without ornament, in the spirit of Frank Lloyd Wright and Mies van der Rohe: long, clean horizontal slabs of stone cantilevered out of the living rock over open air, deep overhangs, bands of windows, crisp right angles, every surface plain and perfectly made; it is beautiful because it works, never because it is decorated.

Palette: pale grey granite, warm honey-coloured stone, the green of planted terraces, white water, snow and dark pine.

People here wear dwarves: short, broad, sturdy people with neat practical beards or braids, sleeves rolled up, leather work aprons and perfectly made plain work clothes in undyed and earthy tones, always busy at a task; any armour is plain, smooth, polished steel plate with no decoration. Human and other traders come and go, buying and selling, then leaving.

Do not draw: boxy whitewashed hill-town cubes, thin walkways in place of the gate, pueblo adobe, carved ornament, runes, gold trim, giant statues, fantasy dwarf halls with pillars and braziers, grim iron doors, organic curves or Gaudí shapes.

Style: Sword-and-sorcery comic art in the spirit of 1970s-80s Conan the Barbarian and Masters of the Universe: bold confident ink outlines, dramatic lighting, saturated flat colours with hard cel shading and halftone-dot shading, pulpy and dramatic. No text, no logos, no speech bubbles.

Composition: a tight crop from the middle of a larger illustration, so the artwork runs off all four edges of the image. Nothing surrounds the art: no border, no white or cream margin, no paper, no frame, no panel outline.
